articles.title: From idea to speech

body.support:
Having your say means getting people to listen. Here's how.

**1. Pick your issue.** Choose something you care about. Who do you need to convince?

**2. Your point of view.** Say it in one sentence. That's your **contention**.

**3. Reasons and proof.** Give two reasons. Back each one with **evidence**: a fact or example. Say where it came from.

**4. Set it out.**

- **Hook:** grab them.
- **Your view.**
- **Reasons**, with evidence.
- **“Some people say… but…”**
- **What you want them to do.**

**5. Cue cards.** Write key words, not every word.

**6. Say it well.** Stand tall. Look up. Slow down. Pause.

**7. Questions.** Listen to the whole question. Pause. Answer short. If you don't know, say: *“I'll find out.”*

**8. Look back.** What worked? What will you change?
body.core:
Having your say is about more than having an opinion. It's about getting people to listen, and to act. Here's how to go from an idea to a speech that works.

**1. Pick your issue and audience.** Choose something you actually care about: your town, your workplace, your sport, your future. Then ask: *who needs convincing?* A school council, an employer, classmates, the local council?

**2. Write your contention.** Your **contention** is your point of view in one sentence. *“Riverside needs a late-night weekend bus.”* If you can't say it in one sentence, you're not ready yet.

**3. Find reasons and evidence.** Choose two or three strong reasons. Back each one with **evidence**: a fact, a number, an example or an expert. Use reliable sources, and say where your information comes from: *“According to the council's youth survey…”*

**4. Structure it.**

- **Hook:** a question, story or surprising fact.
- **Contention:** your point of view.
- **Reasons:** each with evidence. Signpost them: *“My first reason…”*
- **Rebuttal:** *“Some people say ___. But ___.”*
- **Call to action:** what you want them to do.

**5. Use cue cards, not a script.** Write key words only, one card per section. Mark where to pause and look up.

**6. Deliver it.** Stand tall. Make eye contact. Slow down. Pause before your big points. Let your voice rise and fall.

**7. Handle questions.** Listen to the whole question. Pause. Thank them if it fits. Answer briefly, with evidence if you can. If you don't know, say so: *“That's a good question. I'll find out.”* Stay calm, even if the question is tough.

**8. Look back.** Record your speech if you can. What worked? What would you change?
body.extend:
Having your say means more than holding an opinion. It means persuading an audience to listen, and to act. Here's how to move from an idea to an effective speech.

**1. Define your issue and audience.** Choose an issue you genuinely care about. Then identify who needs persuading: a school council, an employer, peers, a local council.

**2. Frame your contention.** Your **contention** is your position in one sentence: *“Riverside needs a late-night weekend bus.”* If you can't state it simply, refine it.

**3. Build reasons with evidence.** Select two or three strong reasons, each supported by relevant, reliable **evidence**: data, examples or expert views. **Acknowledge** your sources aloud (*“According to the council's 2026 youth survey…”*) and keep a reference list.

**4. Structure the speech.**

- **Hook:** an anecdote, question or striking fact.
- **Contention.**
- **Reasons:** signposted and supported.
- **Rebuttal:** anticipate the strongest objection and answer it.
- **Call to action:** a specific request.

**5. Prepare cue cards.** Use key words, not a script, and mark delivery cues: pauses, emphasis, LOOK UP.

**6. Deliver with control.** Use posture, eye contact, pace, pauses and intonation deliberately.

**7. Respond to questions.** Listen to the full question, pause, and answer concisely with evidence. Acknowledge limits honestly: *“I don't have that figure, but I'll find out.”* Stay composed under challenge.

**8. Evaluate.** Review a recording against clear criteria, and identify specific improvements.

caseStudies.title: From Youth Parliament to free travel

body.support:
Every year, young Victorians go to **Parliament House** for **Youth Parliament**. They write ideas for new laws. Then they debate them.

In **2024**, a team argued that students should ride public transport for **free**. Their idea passed.

In **2025**, the Victorian Government said it would make public transport free for everyone under 18. It started on **1 January 2026**. More than **one million** young people can now travel free.

The YMCA says the idea started at Youth Parliament.

Young people stood up, made their case, and it happened. Your voice counts.
body.core:
Every year, the **YMCA Victoria Youth Parliament** brings young Victorians to **Parliament House** in Melbourne. It has run since **1987**. Teams write their own **bills** (ideas for new laws). Then they stand up and debate them, just like real MPs.

Bills that pass Youth Parliament are handed to the **Minister for Youth** and tabled in the real Parliament. That doesn't make them law. But it does put young people's ideas in front of decision-makers.

At the **2024** Youth Parliament, a team from **Boroondara** put forward the **Student Public Transport Concession Bill 2024**. They argued for free public transport for students. The bill passed.

In its **2025/26 Budget**, the Victorian Government announced free public transport for everyone under 18. On **1 January 2026**, it began. Young Victorians can now ride trains, trams and buses for free with a Youth myki. The government said more than **one million** young people were eligible.

YMCA Victoria says the idea started at Youth Parliament. The government's announcements didn't mention it. Either way, young people had stood up in Parliament House, argued for it with evidence, and won the vote, before it became real.

Other ideas debated at Youth Parliament have also helped shape laws over the years. The Victorian Government has named laws on bike helmets and roadside drug testing.
body.extend:
Since **1987**, the **YMCA Victoria Youth Parliament** has brought young Victorians to **Parliament House** each year. Teams write their own **bills**, then debate them in the chambers under real parliamentary rules.

Bills that pass are handed to the **Minister for Youth** and tabled in the Victorian Parliament. That doesn't make them law. But it puts young people's ideas in front of decision-makers.

At the **2024** Youth Parliament, a team from **Boroondara** introduced the **Student Public Transport Concession Bill 2024**. It argued for free public transport for students. The bill passed.

In its **2025/26 Budget**, the Victorian Government announced free public transport for everyone under 18. It began on **1 January 2026**. Young people can now ride trains, trams and buses for free with a Youth myki. The government said more than **one million** young Victorians were eligible.

YMCA Victoria says the policy started at Youth Parliament. The government's announcements didn't mention it. Either way, young people had made the case formally, with evidence, and won a vote before the policy was adopted.

The Victorian Government has also said that earlier Youth Parliament bills helped shape laws on bike helmets and roadside drug testing.

model.text:
**Issue:** Apprentices should get help with the cost of tools.

**Hook:** “On my first day, my boss gave me a list. It came to $1,400. I was earning $14 an hour.”

**Contention:** First-year apprentices need more help to buy tools.

**Evidence 1:** My own tool list and receipts.
**Evidence 2:** First-year pay rates from the Fair Work pay guide.
**Evidence 3:** What three other apprentices at my TAFE told me.

**Call to action:** Ask our local MP to back tool support for first years.

**Questions I might get:** “Don't employers supply tools?” Some do. Many don't.

teacher.overview: The Have Your Say boss level. Students plan, prepare and deliver a two- to three-minute persuasive speech on an issue they care about, with evidence and acknowledged sources, a clear structure (hook, contention, reasons, rebuttal, call to action), cue cards with delivery notes, and controlled delivery. They prepare for and answer audience questions. The case study is the YMCA Victoria Youth Parliament: a 2024 bill for free student public transport passed, and free travel for all under-18s began on 1 January 2026.
prep: If possible, arrange a real audience: the school council, SRC, a teacher panel, or a local council youth officer.
Provide index cards for cue cards.
Have a list of issue ideas ready for students who get stuck (local transport, school facilities, youth jobs, a sport or club issue).

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** a contention is your point of view in one sentence (e.g. Riverside needs a late-night weekend bus). Hook, contention, reasons (with evidence), rebuttal, call to action. Listen to the whole question, pause, answer briefly, say you'll find out if you don't know, stay calm.

**Cue cards:** 1 hook; 2 contention; 3 reason with source; 4 second reason (signposted, slow); 5 rebuttal; 6 call to action.

**Case study:** the 2024 team argued for free student public transport; the bill passed; the government announced free travel for under-18s in its 2025/26 Budget, starting 1 January 2026. Answers will vary on why the government didn't credit it (e.g. it was a budget decision with many inputs).

realityCheck: **Choosing an issue is the hardest part.** Give a list; let students speak about work, sport or their town.
**Real audiences raise the stakes, in a good way.** Even one guest makes it feel real.
**Questions scare students most.** Practise them in pairs first.
**Keep recordings private.** They're for self-evaluation, not sharing.
**Works in a real class:** yes. A strong finish to Unit 2, and good practice for the capstones.
